Some upgrades to public infrastructure may experience opposition from the community due to aesthetic or environmental reasons, or worries about resources. 14 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications 4 Conclusion Legacy device replacement across grid, transportation, and building systems represents a complex challenge that extends far beyond simple equipment obsolescence. As this analysis has demonstrated, replacement decisions are driven by interconnected factors including supply chain constraints, physical degradation, evolving feature require- ments, budgetary limitations, and public perception. Understanding these drivers and their interactions is essential for developing effective modernization strategies that balance technical performance, economic feasibility, and stakeholder acceptance. The replacement patterns identified across sectors reveal significant differences in lifecycle timelines and degradation mechanisms. Grid infrastructure often operates for decades before encountering critical limitations, while transportation and building systems face more immediate pressures from environmental exposure and evolving technological standards. These varying timelines necessitate sector-specific approaches to infrastructure planning and resource allocation. 4.1 Pathway Forward Effective legacy device modernization requires coordinated action across multiple stakeholders and decision-making levels. The following priorities can help guide strategic planning and implementation: • Coordinated Infrastructure Planning: Utilities, municipalities, and building operators must work collab- oratively to align grid upgrades with building and transportation system improvements. This coordination is particularly critical as DERs, EVs, and advanced building controls increase the complexity of grid-building interactions. Joint planning efforts can identify opportunities for shared infrastructure investments and avoid costly misalignments between system capabilities. • Strategic Incentive Programs: Targeted incentive programs for building upgrades can accelerate the adop- tion of smart technologies while addressing equity concerns. These programs should prioritize cost-effective improvements that deliver multiple benefits—such as energy efficiency, grid flexibility, and enhanced com- fort—while ensuring that lower-income households are not left behind in the transition to modern infrastruc- ture. • Cross-Sector Research and Development: Continued research is needed to address persistent challenges in legacy device integration, cybersecurity, interoperability standards, and lifecycle management. Priority areas include: – Development of secure communication protocols that can bridge legacy and modern systems. – Standardization efforts to reduce compatibility barriers across equipment generations. – Advanced forecasting tools to better predict equipment degradation and optimize replacement timing. – Cost-benefit frameworks that account for the full value of modernization, including reliability, flexibility, and resilience benefits. • Proactive Supply Chain Management: Organizations should develop strategies to mitigate supply chain risks for both legacy equipment maintenance and new technology deployment.
